chunks: What to route on inner vs outer layers. The question: What should be routed on each layer? What should be routed on inner layers vs top/bottom layer?
The outer layers of a board and the inner layers behave differently, so what you route where matters. Outer layers touch the parts, the test probes and the air.
Inner layers are buried between solid copper planes. Put short links, parts and anything you need to probe on the outside.
Put long, fast or noisy signals on the inside, where the planes contain them.
Think of a desk and a drawer. Papers on the desk are easy to reach, but a spill can reach them too.
Papers in the drawer are protected and tidy, but each trip in or out takes effort. Outer-layer traces are on the desk.
Inner-layer traces are in the drawer, and each trip in or out costs a via.
The analogy is loose on one point: an inner trace is protected by planes above and below it, not just by a lid.
An example assignment on the 6-layer stack from "Choosing a board stackup".
The signals that must reach parts stay outside; the long, fast ones are inside between a ground and a power plane.
Via: a plated hole that takes a trace from one layer to another. Microstrip: an outer trace with one plane below it and air above ("Layers for high-speed signal routing").
Stripline: an inner trace with a plane above and a plane below it. Return path: the plane area carrying the signal's current back ("Which layers should be ground").
Skew: a timing difference between signals that should arrive together.
Signals travel at different speeds on the two layer types. On an outer layer part of the field is in air, so a signal takes about 6.
0 picoseconds (trillionths of a second) per mm. On an inner layer the field is all in the board material, so it takes about 6. 9 picoseconds/mm.
Over 100 mm that is 600 picoseconds against 690 picoseconds, a 90 picoseconds gap.
At 10 Gb/s (ten billion bits per second) one bit lasts only 100 picoseconds, so two signals that must arrive together cannot be split across layer types.
Keep each group on the same layers. That is the whole idea.
"Outer layers are for component access: fanouts, short links, test points, RF tuning and power pours.
Inner signal layers, between planes, are for long runs and fast or noisy signals, because the field stays inside the board, so there's less emission and pickup.

I route adjacent signal layers orthogonally to cut crosstalk, keep each bus or differential pair on one layer type to avoid skew from the different propagation speeds, and always give the signal a continuous plane next to it."
